Also save a combined markdown version with `## Appendix:` header added at the end. ### Pitfalls - **PDF extraction quality**: `pdftotext` may mangle columns, tables, or complex layouts. Always review the extracted text for artifact lines (page numbers, TOC lists, header/footer repeats). - **Second TOC**: When adding an appendix, update the TOC to include it. If there are TWO TOCs (one in markdown, one programmatic), remove the programmatic one to avoid duplicates. - **Back cover CSS isolation**: The `.back-cover` styles must NOT inherit from the body styles. Use explicit `color: #ffffff` and `background-color: #000000` to guarantee visual independence from the book's interior CSS. - **File size**: Appending a large external document can double the manuscript size. Verify the generated HTML still renders within reasonable load times. ## KDP Print-Ready PDF Generation When a user needs a print-ready PDF for KDP paperback, generate a version with **bleeds** — the print area extends 0.125" beyond the trim on each edge. ### Technique: WeasyPrint with Bleed CSS Start from the same HTML used for the ebook, but modify the CSS: ```css /* KDP Print-Ready: 6x9in + 0.125in bleed */ @page { size: 6.25in 9.25in; /* 6x9 + 0.125in bleed on each side */ margin: 0.75in; /* safe margin inside bleed */ @top-center { content: "BOOK TITLE"; font-family: 'Times New Roman', Times, serif; font-size: 8pt; color: #999; } @bottom-center { content: counter(page); font-family: 'Times New Roman', Times, serif; font-size: 9pt; color: #666; } } @page:first { @top-center { content: none; } @bottom-center { content: none; } } ``` **Important:** Remove the front cover page from the interior PDF (KDP uses the wrap cover as the cover, so the interior starts with the title page). Strip the cover div before generating the print PDF: ```python # Remove front cover from interior (KDP uses wrap cover) html = re.sub(r'.*?', '', html, flags=re.DOTALL) ``` ### Full KDP Package Bundling When asked for a "KDP package" or "everything to publish," build a structured ZIP with both Kindle and Print subdirectories: ```python PKG_DIR = Path("BookName_KDP_PACKAGE") for d in ["Kindle", "Print", "Marketing_and_Compliance", "Source"]: (PKG_DIR / d).mkdir(parents=True) ``` **Package structure:** ``` BookName_KDP_PACKAGE/ ├── README.md # Upload instructions ├── Kindle/ │ ├── BookName.epub # Kindle manuscript (upload to KDP) │ └── BookName_Cover.jpg # Cover as JPEG (KDP requires .jpg; 1.6:1 ratio e.g. 1600×2560px) │ └── BookName_Cover.png # Cover image (2560px recommended) ├── Print/ │ ├── BookName_Print_Ready.pdf # 6x9in + bleeds │ ├── BookName_Wrap_Cover.png # Full wrap (back + spine + front) │ └── BookName_Cover.png # Front cover ├── Marketing_and_Compliance/ │ ├── Marketing_Copy.md # Description, categories, keywords │ └── KDP_AI_Disclosure.md # AI use record └── Source/ └── BookName_Manuscript.md # Full source ``` ### Marketing Copy Template When generating Marketing_Copy.md, include these specific KDP fields: ```markdown # BOOK TITLE: MARKETING COPY ## Book Title **[Title]: [Subtitle]** ## Author [Name] ## Description (Short - 200 characters) One compelling hook sentence... ## Description (Long - Amazon Style) **Bold hook sentence.** [1-2 paragraphs establishing stakes and value proposition] **Inside you'll discover:** - Bullet 1 - Bullet 2 ... **This book is for you if:** - You run a small business with limited time and budget - ... **What readers are saying:** "Review quote..." ## Categories - BUSINESS & ECONOMICS / Small Business - COMPUTERS / Artificial Intelligence / General - BUSINESS & ECONOMICS / Entrepreneurship (3-5 BISAC categories) ## Keywords (comma-separated) 15-20 relevant keywords... ## Pricing - Kindle eBook: $9.99 - Paperback: $14.99 - Hardcover: $24.99 ## Book Details - Title, Subtitle, Author, Edition, Language, Trim Size, Pages, Publication Date ``` ## Full Wrap Cover Creation (Back + Spine + Front) When preparing a book for print-on-demand (KDP paperback, IngramSpark, etc.), a full wrap cover image is needed — a single wide canvas containing the back cover, spine, and front cover in one piece. ### When to Use - The user requests a "full wrap cover" or "cover with spine and back" for print-on-demand - A paperback/hardcover edition needs retail-ready cover art - The book already has a front cover image and needs matching back + spine panels ### Key Dimensions (for 6×9" trade paperback) | Panel | Width (px) at ~144 DPI | Height (px) | |-------|----------------------|-------------| | Front | 1024 (≈7.1") | 1536 | | Spine | Varies with page count | 1536 | | Back | 1024 | 1536 | | **Full wrap width** | 1024 + spine_px + 1024 | 1536 | **Spine width formula (KDP 50# paper):** `pages × 0.002252 + 0.06` inches - 180 pages: 180 × 0.002252 + 0.06 = 0.465" - 214 pages: 214 × 0.002252 + 0.06 = 0.542" - Convert to px at resolution of front cover: `spine_inches × (cover_width_px / 7.1)` - At ~144 DPI (1024px ÷ 7.1"): `spine_inches × 144` **KDP offers a spine width calculator at** https://kdp.amazon.com/cover-calculator — but the formula above gives the same result for 50# cream/white paper. For thicker paper stocks, use KDP's official calculator. ### Implementation (PIL/Pillow) ```python from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageFont front = Image.open("front_cover.png").convert("RGBA") fw, fh = front.size spine_w = 140 # adjust for actual page count wrap = Image.new("RGBA", (fw + spine_w + fw, fh), (0, 0, 0, 255)) # 1. Back cover (left panel) — black with white text back = Image.new("RGBA", (fw, fh), (0, 0, 0, 255)) draw = ImageDraw.Draw(back) font = ImageFont.truetype("/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSans-Bold.ttf", 32) draw.text((fw//2, 60), "BOOK TITLE", fill=(255,255,255), font=font, anchor="mt") # Draw reviewer blurbs, divider lines, branding... wrap.paste(back, (0, 0), back) # 2. Spine (center panel) spine = Image.new("RGBA", (spine_w, fh), (15, 15, 30, 255)) draw_spine = ImageDraw.Draw(spine) spine_font = ImageFont.truetype(font_path, 20) draw_spine.text((spine_w//2, fh//2), "TITLE • Author", fill=(200,200,200), font=spine_font, anchor="mm") draw_spine.rectangle([3, 0, 5, fh], fill=(180,140,60,200)) # gold accent line wrap.paste(spine, (fw, 0), spine) # 3. Front cover (right panel) — use existing cover art wrap.paste(front, (fw + spine_w, 0), front) wrap.save("Wrap_Cover.png", "PNG", optimize=True) ``` ### Back Cover Content Layout The back cover typically includes (top to bottom): - **Book title** (white, large, centered) - **Subtitle** (light gray, smaller) - **Divider line** (thin, dark gray) - **Review blurbs** (italic, light gray/white, ~16pt) — 2-3 quotes from endorsers - **Reviewer attributions** (smaller, gray) - **Divider line** - **Publisher/imprint branding** (small, bottom) - **ISBN / price** (small, bottom — placeholder or actual) ### Review Blurb Formatting ```python reviews = [ ('"Quote from endorser one. Keep it to 1-2 sentences."', '— Endorser Name, Company'), ('"Quote from endorser two."', '— Endorser Name, Organization'), ] y_start = 150 for quote, author in reviews: draw.text((60, y_start), quote, fill=(220,220,220), font=review_font) draw.text((80, y_start + 100), author, fill=(160,160,160), font=author_font) y_start += 200 # spacing between reviews ``` ### Spine Text For a readable spine on a trade paperback (1"+ spine width), use horizontal text centered on the spine panel. For narrow spines (<1"), text is typically rotated 90 degrees (bottom-to-top). Decision rule: if `spine_w > 180px` at 300 DPI, use horizontal; otherwise use vertical rotated text. ### Font Discovery Always check these common font paths in order, falling through until one exists: ```python for fp in [ "/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSans-Bold.ttf", "/usr/share/fonts/truetype/liberation/LiberationSans-Bold.ttf", "/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSans.ttf", ]: if os.path.exists(fp): font_path = fp break ``` ### Files to Deliver Save the wrap cover alongside the front cover in the publishing package: ``` BookName_FINAL_PACKAGE/ ├── Cover/ │ ├── BookName_Cover.png # Front cover with typography │ └── BookName_Wrap_Cover.png # Full wrap (back + spine + front) ``` --- category: creative related_skills: - openrouter-image-generation - manuscript-preparation-and-delivery requirements: - Python 3.8+ - WeasyPrint (for PDF conversion) - OpenRouter API access (for image generation) - Basic HTML/CSS knowledge - Text editor ", "path": "creative/publishing-workflow/SKILL.md", "skill_dir": "/home/bob/.hermes/skills/creative/publishing-workflow", "linked_files": null, "usage_hint": null, "required_environment_variables": [], "required_commands": [], "missing_required_environment_variables": [], "missing_credential_files": [], "missing_required_commands": [], "setup_needed": false, "setup_skipped": false, "readiness_status": "available"}

Covers: Kindle eBook (EPUB 3), print-ready PDF, wrap cover, marketing copy, AI disclosure, EPUB validation per KDP Kindle Publishing Guidelines 2025.1." category: "publishing" triggers: ["put this on kindle", "prepare for kdp", "kindle package", "book deliverable", "epub", "kindle ebook", "epub validation"] --- # Book Deliverable — KDP Publishing Package Complete workflow for packaging a finished book manuscript for Amazon KDP submission. ## Prerequisites - Finished manuscript (`.md` or `.html`) - Cover image (PNG, any ratio — gets resized) - Output directory containing HTML/EPUB/PDF builds (via your build script) ## Step 0: Pre-Publish Prose Quality Pass Before generating any review PDF or building the KDP package, run an editorial quality pass on the manuscript HTML. Bulk-expanded AI-generated prose often contains generic placeholder paragraphs that undermine reader engagement. ### Quality pass procedure 1. **Load the `manuscript-preparation-and-delivery` skill** and use its `references/generic-paragraph-detection.md` for the full list of generic phrase patterns 2. **Scan the book's HTML** for these patterns: - "The work continued through the long hours" - "In the silence of the habitat" - "The data painted a complex picture" - `"We're making progress," someone reported` - "The implications were staggering" - (full list in the detection reference) 3. **Replace each generic block** with character-driven content: named characters, sensory specifics, dialogue with subtext, emotional stakes. Each replacement should advance the plot or deepen character. 4. **Verify zero generic phrases remain** (allowing for false positives in dialogue) 5. **Verify structural integrity** — chapter headings, TOC, copyright, back matter all still present See `manuscript-preparation-and-delivery/references/generic-paragraph-detection.md` for the bulk replacement script template and before/after examples. ## Step 1: Pre-Publish Review Proof After the quality pass, generate a **content-only review PDF** (no cover artwork) for the author to do a read-through. This catches content and formatting issues before investing time in the full packaging. ### When to use - Author says "send me a review copy" or "I need to read through it first" - Before finalizing cover design — content should be locked first - Before delivering the KDP package ### How to build #### A) From existing print-formatted HTML ```bash weasyprint output/{BOOK_KEY}.html output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf # Verify: 150-200 pages at 6×9in (432×648 pts), all chapters present ``` If the HTML has embedded cover art: ```bash sed '/data:image/d' output/{BOOK_KEY}.html > output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review_Clean.html weasyprint output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review_Clean.html output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf ``` #### B) From raw markdown manuscript (no existing HTML) When starting from a `.md` manuscript, you need to build HTML first. **Always detect the heading format first** — manuscripts do not use a consistent heading level for chapters: **Common heading patterns found across manuscripts:** | Pattern | Example | Frequency | |---------|---------|-----------| | `# Chapter N: Title` | `# Chapter One: The Shock` | Common | | `## Chapter N — Title` | `## Chapter 1 — The Observatory Rising` | Very common | | `## Chapter N: Title` | `## Chapter 1: The Welcome Fleet` | Common | | `# CHAPTER N — TITLE` | `# CHAPTER ONE — BUILT FROM DUST` | Occasional | | `## N. Title` | `## 1. The Artemis Accord` | Rare | | `### Chapter N` | `### Chapter 1` | Rare | **Detection command:** ```bash # Show all unique heading patterns in the manuscript grep -n '^#' manuscript.md | head -30 # Count total chapters grep -c '^## Chapter\|^# Chapter\|^## [0-9]' manuscript.md ``` **Build the review HTML from markdown:** Write a Python script that: 1. Reads the manuscript line-by-line 2. Detects chapter headings (handle both `#` and `##` level headings that contain "Chapter") 3. Wraps each chapter in `

` with `page-break-before: always` 4. Adds title page, copyright page, TOC (list of chapter titles as links), and "About the Author" back matter 5. Applies 6×9in print CSS **Python f-string warning:** When generating HTML via Python in Hermes, use `chr(10).join()` instead of `"\\n".join()` inside f-strings. Python 3.11 (Hermes' runtime) does not allow backslash characters inside f-string `{}` expressions: ```python # WRONG — SyntaxError: x = f'
{"\\n".join(items)}
' # RIGHT: x = f'
{chr(10).join(items)}
' ``` **CSS template for review PDFs:** ```css @page { size: 6in 9in; margin: 0.75in; @bottom-center { content: counter(page); font-size: 9pt; color: #888; } } body { font-family: Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif; line-height: 1.5; font-size: 11pt; } .title-page { text-align: center; padding-top: 30%; } .title-page h1 { font-size: 1.8em; page-break-before: avoid; } h1 { text-align: center; page-break-before: always; font-size: 1.3em; } p { margin: 0.2em 0; text-indent: 1.2em; widows: 2; orphans: 2; } ``` #### C) Preferred — PNG→JPEG for illustrations Replace base64 images with local file paths instead of stripping them. Base64 images are 5× their binary size and slow WeasyPrint to a crawl (a 5-image HTML can be 16+ MB). Convert to `file:///absolute/path/to/image.jpg` references BEFORE creating the review PDF. If the PNG files are large (~750KB each for 1024×1024), convert them to JPEG quality 75-80 to shrink to ~240KB each with negligible visual loss for sketches. #### D) TOC page numbers — hardcode after first pass Replace `target-counter` TOC page numbers with **hardcoded numbers** after the first render pass — `target-counter` is unreliable when long chapter titles wrap (the page number floats to the wrong line). Render → extract actual page numbers via `pdftotext` → hardcode → re-render. #### E) Parallel generation for book series When processing multiple books in a series (e.g., all 5 "No Blue Sky" books), **delegate each book to a separate subagent** via `delegate_task` with parallel tasks. Each subagent independently reads their manuscript and generates the PDF. Max concurrent children defaults to 3 — batch books in groups of 3+2 if needed. ### Verify the review PDF ```bash pdfinfo output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf | grep -E 'Pages|Page size' pdftotext output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf - | grep -c "Chapter" # confirm all chapters present ``` **Page count targeting:** If your book is too short or too long for the target page range (e.g., 180-200 pages at 6×9in), you can adjust the **typography density** (font-size, line-height, margins) to expand or compress the text. See `references/page-count-targeting.md` for the density reference table, CSS knob strengths, and a quick-estimation formula. Apply a different density per book when building a multi-volume series with uneven word counts. **Checklist for author review:** - [ ] All chapters present (count them in the PDF) - [ ] No front cover artwork (just text title page) - [ ] No back cover content - [ ] TOC lists everything - [ ] Page count is reasonable (150-200 for a trade book) - [ ] Final paragraph / closing reflection is present ### Pitfall - WeasyPrint base64 images inside HTML can bloat files to 5MB+. This is fine for PDF generation but slows rendering. Use `sed '/data:image/d'` to strip when cover art isn't needed. - Always verify with `pdfinfo` — WeasyPrint 68+ is stable but `@page` CSS must be present or page dimensions may drift. ## Fast Path: Check for Existing Package First Before building anything, check if a KDP package already exists: ```bash find output/ -name "*_KDP_PACKAGE.zip" -o -type d -name "*_KDP_PACKAGE" | head -5 ``` If found, **verify its specs** before delivering: ```bash # Kindle cover dimensions python3 -c "from PIL import Image; img=Image.open('output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Kindle/{FILE_PREFIX}_Cover.jpg'); print(f'Kindle cover: {img.size}')" # Print PDF page count and trim pdfinfo "output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Print/{FILE_PREFIX}_Print_Ready.pdf" 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'Pages|Page size' # Verify all expected files exist ls output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Kindle/ ls output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Print/ ls output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Marketing_and_Compliance/ ``` **Verified specs should be:** - Kindle cover: **1600×2560** or meets 1.6:1 ratio - Page count: matches expected (~150-200 for typical business/memoir) - Page size: **450×666 pts** (= 6.25×9.25in = 6×9in + 0.125in bleeds) or **432×648 pts** (= 6×9in no bleed) If all pass, skip to **Step 4: Deliver**. Rebuild only if specs are wrong or files are missing. ## Step-by-Step (Build Path) Use this when no existing package exists or it needs rebuilding. ### 1. Check Page Count ```bash pdfinfo output/{FILE_PREFIX}.pdf | grep Pages ``` Or use `PyPDF2.PdfReader`. ### 2. Create Kindle Cover JPEG (1600×2560px) Resize the existing cover to KDP Kindle dimensions (1.6:1 height:width ratio): ```python from PIL import Image img = Image.open('{BOOK_KEY}_Cover.png') resized = img.resize((1600, 2560), Image.LANCZOS) resized.convert('RGB').save('generated_images/{BOOK_KEY}_KDP_Kindle_Cover.jpg', 'JPEG', quality=95) ``` ### 3. Build KDP Package Create `build_kdp_package.py` in the book directory. It should: **a) Kindle/** - Copy the EPUB from `output/` - Copy (or generate) the 1600×2560 Kindle cover JPEG **b) Print/** - Read the existing HTML output - Inject KDP print CSS (6.25×9.25in page with 0.125in bleeds, bleeds margin) - Regenerate PDF via WeasyPrint - Generate wrap cover image (front + spine + back): - Spine width: `pages * 0.00225` (cream paper) or `pages * 0.00252` (white) - Total width: `6.0*2 + spine + 0.125*2` inches - Total height: `9.0 + 0.125*2` inches - At 300 DPI, paste front cover on right, back cover (darkened) on left, spine text centered - Save as JPEG and PDF **c) Marketing_and_Compliance/** - `Book_Description.md` — compelling description (2-3 paragraphs) - `Author_Bio.md` — 2-3 sentence bio - `Categories_and_Keywords.md` — 4 suggested BISAC categories, 7 keywords - `KDP_AI_Disclosure.md` — if AI was used in manuscript generation **d) README.md** — submission instructions for the author **e) ZIP** — archive the entire package ### 4. Deliver to Telegram Send via MEDIA: links: - The `{BOOK_KEY}_KDP_PACKAGE.zip` (full package, under 20MB) - Individual key files as needed ### 5. Save this Skill After completing and noting any issues, patch this skill with fixes. ## KDP Kindle EPUB Requirements (per Kindle Publishing Guidelines 2025.1) **Supporting files:** - `references/kdp-guidelines-sources.md` — all official KDP help topic URLs - `templates/kdp-epub-style.css` — KDP-safe CSS template (no ::before/::after, no counter-*, no img selector) When building the EPUB for Kindle submission, it must comply with Amazon's Kindle Publishing Guidelines. KDP now accepts EPUB3 as the **preferred format** for Kindle eBooks. ### EPUB Structural Requirements | Requirement | Spec | |-------------|------| | Format | **EPUB 3** (preferred), EPUB 2 (acceptable) | | Max file size | **650 MB** including all embedded images | | Validated via | **epubcheck** + **Kindle Previewer 3** (fix all errors AND warnings before upload) | ### EPUB File Structure ``` {Book-Key}.epub/ ├── mimetype ← Must be first file, uncompressed, content: "application/epub+xml" ├── META-INF/ │ └── container.xml ← Points to OPF file └── OEBPS/ ├── content.opf ← Package file with manifest, spine, metadata ├── nav.xhtml ← EPUB 3 nav document (logical TOC, required for books >20 pages) ├── toc.ncx ← EPUB 2 NCX (optional but recommended for backward compat) ├── cover.xhtml ← Cover page ├── title.xhtml ← Title page (optional but recommended) ├── ch01.xhtml ← One XHTML file per chapter ├── ch02.xhtml ├── ... └── images/ ├── cover.jpg ← Internal cover image (JPEG preferred) └── ... ← All chapter images ``` ### 1. Cover Image — Internal (mandatory) - **Must include** Title & Author (no pricing/promotions) - **Must take up ≥50% of allocated space** - Referenced in OPF via preferred method: - `` + manifest item with `properties="cover-image"` - High resolution (see marketing cover specs below) ### 2. Cover Image — Marketing (uploaded separately to KDP) | Property | Spec | |----------|------| | Dimensions | **2560 × 1600 px** (preferred), min 1000 px shortest side | | DPI | 300 ppi minimum | | Format | **JPEG** (preferred), RGB color profile | | Max file size | **5 MB** | | Border | 3–4 px medium gray if background is white/light | | Prohibited | No spine, barcode, back cover, inside flap, watermarks, pricing, promotions | ### 3. It reads a print-formatted\n  HTML manuscript with any of 4+ heading formats (see `references/html-heading-formats.md`),\n  detects chapter boundaries via regex, splits into per-chapter XHTML files, and produces\n  a complete EPUB 3 with embedded cover image, front matter (title page, copyright, TOC),\n  back matter (about the author, series page), nav TOC, NCX, guide items, and KDP-safe CSS.\n  It also generates back-cover text, author bio, and a final ZIP publishing package.\n  Usage:\n  ```bash\n  python3 scripts/html-to-epub.py manuscript.html cover.png "Book Title" "Author" "Series" "1" /output/dir\n  ```\n  Produces: `{Series}_{N}_{Title}.epub` + `{Series}_{N}_{Title}_Publishing_Package.zip`\n  - **Limitation**: Requires `` tags in the HTML for content extraction\n  - **Limitation**: Chapter detection uses regex — works best with consistent heading patterns listed in the reference\n  - **Limitation**: Each chapter becomes one flat XHTML file (no nested sub-sections)\n- **EPUB QA Checker**: Use `scripts/epub-qa.py` to validate any EPUB's structure, content, and\n  compatibility. It checks: mimetype format, ZIP structure, content.opf metadata/manifest/spine,\n  nav.xhtml TOC, toc.ncx, XHTML well-formedness, no scripts, no duplicate IDs, image sizes,\n  and required front/back matter files. Produces pass/fail/warning per book with summary.\n  Usage:\n  ```bash\n  python3 scripts/epub-qa.py [directory with *.epub files]\n  ```\n- **Calibre `ebook-convert`**: For batch conversion, but validate output with epubcheck afterward
  Use `scripts/build-epub-python.py` from this skill's directory. It generates a

  The script creates front matter (title, copyright), back matter (about author),

### 13. KDP-Formats Comparison

    66|## A Note on What You're About to Read
    67|
    68|I wrote this book because I couldn't find it.

    70|Every book on AI agents I could buy was written by someone who advises companies on AI, researches AI at a university, or sells an AI platform. None of them were written by someone who actually runs a business on AI agents. None of them could tell you what it costs to run thirty agents in production, what breaks at 3am, or what happens when your lead-nurturing agent accidentally emails a prospect the wrong thing because a prompt update went sideways.
    71|
    72|I can tell you those things because I built the system, I broke it, and I fixed it. This book is what I learned.

    74|The agents I run handle lead capture, qualification, outreach, scheduling, pipeline tracking, and monitoring at MIFECO. They work 24/7. They cost $380 a month to run. They handle about 90% of the operational work without me touching anything. The remaining 10% . the edge cases, the escalations, the real conversations — that's where I come in.
    75|
    76|That's the model this book teaches. Not theory. Not future-gazing. A working system you can replicate starting this weekend.

    84|# PART I — The Chatbot Trap

    86|## Chapter 1 — The Great AI Disappointment
    87|
    88|My brother-in-law Mark called me six months ago. He runs a mid-sized HVAC company in Phoenix. forty trucks, a hundred and twenty employees, growing fast. He was excited. "We finally got ChatGPT Enterprise," he said. "I set up a whole onboarding assistant. New hires can ask it anything about benefits, PTO, the truck checklist. It took a while but I think we finally have something useful."
    89|
    90|I asked him how it was going. Long pause.
    91|
    92|"Nobody uses it," he said.
    93|
    94|This is the part of the AI story nobody puts in the keynote. Mark spent three weeks with his HR director building custom instructions, uploading policy PDFs, crafting system prompts that ended with "You are a helpful assistant for Apex Cooling & Heating." Three weeks of a founder's and an HR director's time. The chatbot could answer any question about bereavement leave, 401k matching, or which color hard hats are required on job sites. It was comprehensive. It accurately cited page numbers from the employee handbook. It could even adjust its tone based on whether the user was a new hire or a ten-year veteran. It was a technical success. And after the first week, exactly three people had used it. Two of them were the HR director testing it. The third was Mark's brother-in-law who heard about it at dinner and wanted to see what it could do.
    95|
    96|The other was Mark himself, asking it the same questions twice to see if the answers changed.
    97|
    98|I saw the same pattern at my own company, MIFECO, before we pivoted. We built a customer-facing chatbot for our logistics platform. It could tell you shipment status, explain billing, even walk through troubleshooting steps for a stuck conveyor sensor. It was polite, never hallucinated, always apologized for the wait. Our support ticket volume dropped exactly zero percent. People don't want answers. They want their shipment un-stuck. They want the billing error fixed. They want the conveyor running again.
    99|
   100|This is the great AI disappointment of 2024 and 2025. Business owners heard the hype, bought the tools, built the assistants, and got nothing measurable out of them. I talk to founders and operators every week. The pattern is the same: they tried ChatGPT, they tried Claude, they tried the white-label chatbot platforms. Someone in the company spent serious time setting it up. And then nothing happened. No revenue increase. No headcount reduction. No process improvement. Just a chatbot sitting in a corner of the intranet answering questions that nobody was asking.

{"content": "   101|
   102|The gap is between promise and reality. The promise was: AI will transform your business. The reality was: AI gives answers, and your business doesn't need more answers. Your business needs actions.
   103|
   104|Think about what actually runs a business. It's not the knowledge. it's the doing. Every deal that closes required someone to send a proposal. Every happy customer required someone to follow up. Every shipment that arrived on time required someone to check the schedule. Answers are passive. They sit there waiting to be consumed. Actions are active. They change the state of the world.
   105|
   106|A chatbot is a reference library with a friendly face. It's Wikipedia with small talk. It stores information and dispenses it on request. But your business doesn't suffer from a lack of stored information. Your business suffers from a lack of executed work.
   107|
   108|Mark's HVAC company doesn't need an onboarding bot. It needs onboarding to happen: background checks submitted, tool orders placed, truck assignments logged, first-day schedules sent, mentor assignments made. That's a dozen distinct actions per new hire. None of them involve asking a question. All of them involve doing something.
   109|
   110|This realization is what drove the architecture shift at MIFECO. We started with a chatbot for our logistics clients. We ended up building an agent system that takes actions in our platform and in our clients' systems. The difference wasn't the language model. It was the design: we stopped building things that wait for questions and started building things that do work.
   111|
   112|Here's the framework I've developed for thinking about this. Every business process has three layers: knowledge, decision, action. Knowledge is what you know. the policy, the procedure, the data. Decision is the logic that picks what to do given the knowledge. Action is the execution that changes something in the world. ChatGPT handles knowledge perfectly and decision adequately. It handles action not at all.
   113|
   114|If your business problem is knowledge. people don't know the 401k match percentage, people don't know the shipping cutoff time—a chatbot works. But most business problems aren't knowledge problems. They're action problems. The 401k match is known. What's missing is the enrollment form being submitted. The shipping cutoff time is known. What's missing is the order being placed before it.
   115|
   116|The lesson I took from Mark's failed chatbot and from our own early failures is simple: if the AI can't do anything, it doesn't matter how much it knows. Your business runs on actions. Every system you buy, every person you hire, every process you build exists to cause something to happen. If the AI doesn't cause anything to happen, it's not a business tool. It's a parlor trick.
   117|
   118|This book is about the alternative. It's about agents. systems that take action. They don't wait for questions. They follow processes. They use tools. They make decisions within boundaries. They persist across time. And they do work, not just answer questions.
   119|
   120|By the end of this book, you'll know exactly what I mean by that, why it matters for your business, and how to start building it. But first we need to kill the chatbot illusion. You don't need a smarter FAQ. You need a worker that doesn't clock out.
   121|
   122|Mark's chatbot is still running, by the way. It answers three questions a month, all from the HR director. Nobody else bothers. They just call HR like they always did. The tool exists, the knowledge is there, but the behavior hasn't changed. Answers aren't the bottleneck. Action is.
   123|
   124|
   125|## Chapter 2 — Chatbot vs. Agent: Five Differences
   126|
   127|My wife asked me last month what I actually do all day. I said I build agents. She nodded and went back to her phone. A minute later she said, "So like Siri?" The gap between what most people think of as AI and what I'm actually building is wider than most business owners realize. And if you're going to invest in this, you need to see it clearly.
   128|
   129|A chatbot gives answers. An agent takes action. That's the simple version, but the details matter because the details determine what you can actually build. I've identified five practical differences between chatbots and agents that matter for business owners. These aren't academic distinctions. They directly determine whether the thing you build will produce revenue or sit in a forgotten browser tab.
   130|
   131|**First: Memory.**
   132|
   133|ChatGPT has what I call conversation memory. It remembers what you said two messages ago so it can maintain context within a single session. Close the tab, come back, and it's a blank slate. Your business processes don't work that way. A lead reaches out on Monday. Someone follows up on Wednesday. The deal closes two weeks later. Someone needs to remember the lead's company size, budget range, and the specific objection they raised on the first call.
   134|
   135|Agents maintain persistent memory. At MIFECO, our lead outreach agent stores every interaction with every prospect in a structured database. It knows when a prospect asked for pricing but didn't open the follow-up quote. It knows which email templates have been sent, which calls have been scheduled, which objections have been raised. This isn't clever prompting. It's architecture. The agent writes to a database and reads from it before every action. It remembers because we built memory into the system, not because a language model happened to keep something in context.
   136|
   137|The business implication is huge. Without persistent memory, every interaction is a first date. You can't build relationships, you can't track progress, you can't learn from past failures. A chatbot that forgets everything between sessions isn't useful for anything beyond answering the same question twice.
   138|
   139|**Second: Autonomy.**
   140|
   141|Every chatbot waits for a question. That's the fundamental design. The user types, the chatbot answers. The user stops typing, the chatbot stops existing. It's purely reactive.
   142|
   143|Agents are proactive within their defined scope. Our pipeline outreach agent doesn't wait for someone to ask it to follow up. At 10 AM every day, it checks the schedule. If a prospect hasn't responded in three days, it sends a follow-up email. If a response comes in with certain keywords, it routes it to a human. If the prospect said "call me next week," it creates a calendar reminder and waits.
   144|
   145|This changes the economics of the system. A chatbot removes maybe a minute per question that someone would have spent searching. An agent removes entire workflows. Nobody has to remember to follow up. Nobody has to check whether the lead went cold. The agent just does it because that's how it was built.
   146|
   147|**Third: Tool Use.**
   148|
   149|ChatGPT can generate text. That's it. It can generate really good text, but it can't do anything else. It can't send an email, update a CRM record, schedule a meeting, run a report, or change a setting.
   150|
   151|An agent uses tools. Our MIFECO agent has a set of capabilities: send email via our email API, create a contact in HubSpot, check calendar availability, generate a proposal PDF from a template, post a message to Slack. When the agent decides a prospect needs a proposal, it doesn't output a proposal draft for a human to copy-paste. It generates the PDF and sends it. The action completes.
   152|
   153|This is the single biggest difference in practical terms. A chatbot says "here's the answer." An agent says "I took care of it." One produces text. The other produces results.
   154|
   155|**Fourth: Persistence.**
   156|
   157|Chatbots exist only when someone is talking to them. They have no presence in your system outside of active conversations. They don't monitor. They don't watch. They don't trigger.
   158|
   159|Agents run continuously. Our lead qualification agent runs 24/7. It monitors our intake forms, our email inbox, and our calendar system. When a new lead submits a form, the agent is already processing it within seconds. It doesn't require someone to start a conversation. It's always there, watching its assigned territory.
   160|
   161|Think of it like a security guard versus an alarm system. A chatbot is a security guard who only works when you're standing in front of him asking questions. An agent is an alarm system that watches all the time and only alerts you when something happens.
   162|
   163|**Fifth: Decision-Making.**
   164|
   165|ChatGPT makes exactly one decision: what words to say next. It's a text prediction engine dressed up as intelligence. It's excellent at that, but it's also incredibly limited.
   166|
   167|Agents make operational decisions. Should I follow up now or wait? Should I route this to sales or support? Should I escalate to a human or handle it myself? These decisions require evaluation against rules, priorities, and business logic. The language model informs the decision, but the decision framework is separate.
   168|
   169|At MIFECO, our agent evaluates leads against a scoring model. If the lead is from a company with more than fifty employees and has visited the pricing page, the agent schedules a demo call. If the lead is from a company under ten employees and asked a general question, the agent sends an info packet. The language model generates the email text. The decision framework determines what happens. This separation is critical. You can change the rules without rewriting the prompts.
   170|
   171|The practical difference between all five of these capabilities is straightforward. A chatbot is a tool you use. An agent is a worker you manage. You use a hammer. You manage an employee. The relationship is different, the expectations are different, and the results are different.
   172|
   173|When you use a chatbot, you do the work of framing the question, interpreting the answer, and taking the action. The chatbot supports you while you do the work. When you manage an agent, you define the scope, set the boundaries, and review the results. The agent does the work.
   174|
   175|Most businesses that tried AI got a chatbot and expected an agent. They expected the AI to do work. Instead, they got a tool that produces text they still had to act on. No wonder they were disappointed.
   176|
   177|The five differences. memory, autonomy, tool use, persistence, decision-making—are the specification sheet for an agent system. If you're evaluating a vendor, building an internal tool, or just trying to understand what's possible, these are the five questions to ask. Does it remember between sessions? Does it act without being asked? Can it change things in the world? Does it run continuously? Does it make operational decisions or just generate text?
   178|
   179|If the answer to any of those is no, you're looking at a chatbot. And you already know what that gets you.
   180|
   181|
   182|## Chapter 3 — Why Your CRM Can't Save You
   183|
   184|In 2022, MIFECO spent forty-three thousand dollars on Salesforce. License fees, implementation consultant, custom fields, integrations with HubSpot and Mailchimp. Six months later, our sales pipeline looked exactly the same as it did before. Same number of leads. Same conversion rate. Same revenue. The only thing that changed was we had a really expensive database that nobody wanted to update.
   185|
   186|I'm not here to pick on Salesforce. Pick your poison. HubSpot, Pipedrive, Zoho, Freshsales. They're all the same thing: a database with a nice interface and some automation features bolted on. They're useful. I'm not saying you shouldn't have one. But if you think your CRM is going to solve your pipeline problems, you're wrong. Here's why.
   187|
   188|CRMs require data entry. That's their fundamental design constraint. The system doesn't know anything unless a human tells it. A lead calls, you take notes, you log the call. A prospect visits your pricing page, you log the visit. A deal progresses, you update the stage. Every piece of information in your CRM was put there by someone typing.
   189|
   190|This creates what I call the CRM maintenance tax. Every time someone enters data, they're not selling. Every minute spent updating fields, moving deals between stages, logging activities is a minute taken from actual revenue-generating work. Salespeople feel this. That's why CRM adoption rates hover around fifty percent in most organizations. The people who are supposed to use it don't want to, because using it takes time away from what they're measured on.
   191|
   192|The result is a database that's never quite accurate. Leads slip through because nobody logged the call. Deals sit in the wrong stage because nobody updated it. Follow-ups get missed because nobody set the reminder. The CRM becomes an aspirational record. what the sales team wishes was happening, not what's actually happening.
   193|
   194|At MIFECO, we ran into this hard. We were using HubSpot to manage our logistics platform leads. A prospect would fill out the contact form, HubSpot would create a contact record, and then nothing. The contact would sit there until someone on our three-person sales team noticed it and did something. Sometimes that was ten minutes. Sometimes it was three days. Sometimes never. One lead came in on a Friday afternoon. The salesperson noticed it the following Wednesday. By then the prospect had already signed a contract with a competitor. I still have the email the prospect sent us when we finally called: "We reached out to you twice and never heard back. We went with someone else."
   195|
   196|We analyzed six months of HubSpot data and found that thirty-seven percent of inbound leads never received any follow-up at all. Not a call. Not an email. Nothing. They filled out the form and went into the void. Those leads cost us money. we were paying for ads to generate them.
   197|
   198|The problem wasn't that we had the wrong CRM. The problem was that the CRM couldn't do anything. It could store a lead. It could show us a list of leads that needed attention. It could even send a notification. But it couldn't call the lead. It couldn't send a personalized email. It couldn't check whether we'd already sent a proposal. It couldn't follow up. It just sat there, a filing cabinet full of opportunities we were too busy to pursue.
   199|
   200|This is where agents change the equation. An agent doesn't need data entry because it performs data entry itself. It generates the information it needs through its own actions. Our lead agent doesn't wait for a salesperson to log a call. It makes the call, records the outcome, stores the notes, and updates the deal stage. The CRM becomes a byproduct of the agent's work, not the bottleneck.
   201|
   202|Think about the difference in information flow. In a CRM-dependent system, information flows like this: event happens, human notices, human opens CRM, human types information, information is stored. There are four handoffs, and three of them require human attention.
   203|
   204|In an agent-driven system, information flows like this: event happens, agent detects event, agent takes action, agent records action. One continuous process.
   205|
   206|The financial implications are direct. Every hour your sales team spends updating CRM fields is an hour they don't spend selling. If your average salesperson's fully loaded cost is one hundred thousand dollars a year, and they spend fifteen percent of their time on data entry, that's fifteen thousand dollars of lost selling capacity per person. For a team of ten, that's a hundred and fifty thousand dollars a year. That's not the cost of the CRM. That's the cost of the CRM's design limitation.
   207|
   208|But the bigger cost is the pipeline leaks that happen because the CRM can't act. Those thirty-seven percent of uncontacted leads at MIFECO represented about sixty-two thousand dollars in potential revenue per month that we were systematically losing. Not because we didn't know they existed. We knew. HubSpot showed them to us. We just couldn't get to them.
   209|
   210|An agent doesn't have that problem. An agent can contact every lead. It doesn't get tired, it doesn't get busy, it doesn't prioritize the squeaky wheel. It processes the list. Every lead gets contacted. Every follow-up gets sent. Every deal stage gets updated.
   211|
   212|I'm not saying you should throw out your CRM. We still use one at MIFECO. But we use it as a data store, not as an operations system. The CRM holds the records. The agent does the work. The CRM documents what happened. The agent makes things happen.
   213|
   214|If you're evaluating whether an agent system would help your business, look at your CRM first. Not at what it shows you. Look at what it's not showing you. the deals that should be there but aren't, the follow-ups that were supposed to happen but didn't, the leads that came in and disappeared. That gap between what your CRM says and what your pipeline actually needs is exactly where an agent earns its keep.
   215|
   216|The CRM can't save you because the CRM is a record of what happened. You don't need a better record. You need better execution.
   217|
   218|
   219|## Chapter 4 — The Real Cost of Manual Workflows
   220|
   221|I spent a week doing a time audit at MIFECO. Not the kind where you estimate. The kind where I ran a timer and tracked every single thing I did for five days. The results were embarrassing. Thirty-seven percent of my working time went to tasks that could be done by a well-designed script. Copying data from one system to another. Checking whether someone had done something they were supposed to do. Following up on things I already followed up on. Reconciling numbers that should have matched the first time.
   222|
   223|I'm not unusual. I've talked to dozens of founders and operators who've done similar audits. The numbers are consistent. Somewhere between twenty and forty percent of every knowledge worker's day is spent on tasks that are repetitive, rules-based, and require no creative judgment. We call this work. It's not. It's overhead.
   224|
   225|The problem is that we don't feel the cost day to day. You don't write a check for context switching. Nobody invoices you for mental overhead. The costs are invisible, which is why they're so dangerous. They accumulate silently, and they compound over time.
   226|
   227|Let me give you specific numbers from MIFECO. We had a process for onboarding new logistics clients. It involved twelve steps: send the welcome email, create the account, configure the portal access, set up the notification preferences, upload the asset list, schedule the training call, send the API documentation, create the support ticket template, add the contact to the weekly status list, send the invoice for setup fees, confirm the payment, and send the welcome packet. Twelve steps. Each step required someone to open a different tool, find the right record, fill out a form, and move on.
   228|
   229|The first time you do this, it takes about forty minutes. The tenth time, it takes about thirty minutes. The hundredth time, it still takes about twenty-five minutes. You get faster, but you never get fast, because most of the time is spent navigating between systems, not thinking.
   230|
   231|We had two people spending about eight hours a week each on client onboarding. That's sixteen hours a week.    233|But the direct labor cost is only half the story. The real cost was what those two people couldn't do because they were doing onboarding.    234|
   235|This is the hidden cost of manual workflows: opportunity cost. Every hour you spend doing something a machine could do is an hour you don't spend doing something only a human can do. Building relationships. Solving novel problems. Making strategic decisions. Improving your product.
   236|
   237|I call this the manual workflow tax. It has four components.
   238|
   239|The first is the execution cost. This is the direct time spent performing the work. Copying the email, pasting it, clicking save. That's the visible cost, and it's usually the smallest.

   246|

   249|The total time savings was about fifteen hours per week. At fifty dollars an hour, that's seven hundred and fifty dollars per week, or thirty-nine thousand dollars per year.    250|
   251|If you want to find where agents can help your business, start with the work nobody wants to do. The tasks that people put off. The processes that have checklists.    252|
   253|The real cost of manual workflows isn't the labor. It's the lost potential of using your people for things that actually matter.
   254|
   255|
   256|## Chapter 5 — The Pipeline Problem
   257|
   258|I lost a seventy-three thousand dollar deal in 2023 because nobody followed up. The lead came in through our website. A logistics manager at a mid-size distribution company filled out the contact form, said they were evaluating platforms, and asked for a demo. The email landed in our shared inbox. Someone routed it to the right salesperson. And then nothing happened for eleven days.
   259|
   260|When we finally called, they had already signed with a competitor. The prospect told us later, "We figured you weren't interested." We were interested. We were just disorganized.
   261|
   262|This is the pipeline problem. It's not a lead generation problem. It's not a product problem. It's a follow-up problem. Your business generates leads through marketing, referrals, inbound. Those leads have value. They represent people who have raised their hand and said, "I might pay you money." And then your business systematically fails to convert them because the process of moving from hand-raise to closed deal requires consistent, timely, persistent action.
   263|
   264|The data on response time is brutal. Harvard Business Review published a study a few years ago showing that companies that contacted potential customers within an hour of receiving an inquiry were nearly seven times more likely to qualify the lead than those that waited even an hour.    265|
   266|Most businesses don't respond within an hour. Most businesses don't respond within twenty-four hours. MIFECO didn't. Our average response time was about forty-seven hours. That wasn't because we were bad at our jobs. It was because the leads arrived into a system that required a human to notice them, prioritize them, and act. Humans have other things to do. Sales calls. Internal meetings. Lunch. The leads pile up.
   267|
   268|The relationship between response time and close rate isn't linear. It drops off a cliff. The first hour is golden. The first day is workable.    269|
   270|At MIFECO, we traced the revenue impact of this. Over a six-month period, we received four hundred and twelve inbound leads. Our sales team contacted two hundred and sixty of them. So we left about a hundred and fifty-two thousand dollars on the table from leads we didn't contact at all. And probably another fifty thousand from leads we contacted too late.
   271|
   272|This wasn't a sales team problem. We had good salespeople. They were busy. They focused on the leads that seemed most promising. They followed up with the people who followed up with them. The leads that required proactive outreach. the ones that came in, requested information, and waited to hear back—those fell through the cracks because nobody had a systematic process for handling them.
   273|
   274|I built a lead agent at MIFECO to solve this. It's not complicated. The agent monitors our contact form and our inbound email. When a new lead arrives, it checks the information against our ideal customer profile. Company size, industry, role. It assigns a score.    275|
   276|The response time dropped from forty-seven hours to ninety seconds. Not because we hired more people. Because the agent responded within ninety seconds of every submission, regardless of time of day, regardless of whether the sales team was in a meeting or on vacation.
   277|

   279|
   280|The most surprising result was what happened with the leads we used to ignore. The low-scoring ones. The small companies, the general inquiries, the people who didn't fit our ideal profile. Before the agent, those leads got nothing. After the agent, they got an automated response with information about our platform and an invitation to sign up for a self-service trial.    281|
   282|The lesson here is uncomfortable. Most businesses don't have a pipeline problem. They have a pipeline leak problem. The top of the funnel is fine. Marketing generates leads. Referrals generate leads. Inbound generates leads. But somewhere between the lead arriving and the deal closing, the water drains out. It drains through inconsistent follow-up. It drains through slow response times. It drains through the absence of systematic process.
   283|
   284|Fixing this with people is expensive. You can hire more salespeople, but they'll prioritize the same way. They'll focus on the big deals, the easy conversations, the people who chase them back. They'll let the small leads go. They'll take weekends off. They'll get busy with internal meetings.
   285|
   286|An agent doesn't prioritize that way. An agent processes every lead the same way, according to the rules you set. It doesn't get tired. It doesn't get distracted. It doesn't decide a lead is too small to bother with. It just executes the process.
   287|
   288|I'm not saying agents replace salespeople. They don't. Our sales team still handles the complex conversations, the negotiations, the relationship building.    289|
   290|The pipeline problem is a throughput problem. Your funnel leaks because you can't keep up with the volume.
