{"content": "   701|Talking means the agent says something. It drafts an email, generates a summary, answers a question. Talking is low risk. The worst outcome is that the agent says something slightly wrong and a human corrects it.
   702|
   703|Acting means the agent changes something. It submits a form, updates a database record, sends a message, creates an invoice. Acting is high risk. The worst outcome is that the agent does something irreversible.
   704|
   705|My rule: default to talking, escalate to acting only when the cost of inaction exceeds the cost of a mistake.
   706|
   707|The lead responder talks. it drafts emails. It does not act—it does not send them. The logistics coordinator talks—it suggests delivery window changes. It acts on one thing—logging tracking events, which is low-risk and high-frequency.
   708|
   709|Your agents should follow the same pattern. Give them plenty of talking tools. Give them acting tools sparingly, with approval gates, and with hard permission enforcement at the integration layer, not the agent layer. The agent can suggest anything it wants. The tool system only executes what is allowed.
   710|
   711|## Chapter 15 — Human-in-the-Loop
   712|
   713|The question I get most often from other founders is not about technology. It is about trust. "How do I know the agent will not screw something up?" The answer is that you do not know. So you design for that uncertainty.
   714|
   715|I use three modes for agent operation. Full auto, where the agent acts without approval. Approve-first, where the agent proposes and a human authorizes. Review-after, where the agent acts immediately and a human inspects the result later. Each mode serves a different function. Picking the wrong mode for a given function is where the real failures happen.
   716|
   717|Full auto is for actions where speed matters more than perfection, and the cost of a mistake is low. At MIFECO, our monitoring agent runs in full auto. It checks system health metrics every five minutes. If it detects an anomaly. CPU spike, error rate jump, queue backlog—it creates a diagnostic report and posts it to our incident channel. It does not ask permission. It just does it. The cost of a false alarm is a few seconds of reading time. The cost of a missed alarm is a production outage. Full auto is the right call.
   718|
   719|Another full auto example is our logging agent. Every agent run is logged with a structured record: prompt, tool calls, decisions, outcome. The logging agent writes these to the database automatically. If it wrote a bad record, I would notice in the weekly review. If it failed to write a record, I would have no audit trail. Full auto ensures the audit trail exists.
   720|
   721|Approve-first is for actions where accuracy matters and a human can add value by reviewing before execution. This is where most of our agents operate. The lead responder drafts emails but does not send them until Jenny approves. The contract reviewer flags unusual clauses but does not suggest redlines until legal reviews. The escalation handler proposes a resolution path but does not execute it until the shift lead confirms.
   722|
   723|Approve-first adds latency. The lead responder's email sits in a queue for an average of forty minutes before someone reviews it. That is forty minutes slower than a fully automated system. But it is also forty minutes of protection against the kind of mistake that costs a customer relationship.
   724|
   725|I learned this the hard way. Early on, I ran the lead responder in full auto mode for a week. It sent one hundred and thirty-seven emails. One of them contained a pricing hallucination. The agent quoted a price thirty percent below our actual rate. The lead replied and wanted to buy at that price. We had to honor it because the email was sent from our domain. That mistake cost us about twelve hundred dollars in margin. Approve-first would have caught it because Jenny would have seen the price and corrected it before send.
   726|
   727|Review-after is for actions where execution speed is critical and the review can happen asynchronously. Our logistics coordinator runs in review-after mode. When a shipment is delayed, the agent updates the delivery window in the customer portal immediately. Then it flags the update for review. The logistics team checks the flagged updates at the end of each shift. By then, most customers have already seen the updated window and adjusted their plans. If the update was wrong, the team corrects it and the customer gets a notification. The cost of a wrong update is a correction. The benefit of an immediate update is customer trust.
   728|
   729|The framework I use to decide which mode to use has three variables.
   730|
   731|First variable: reversibility. Can the action be undone? Sending an email is irreversible. Updating a lead score is reversible. Creating a support ticket is reversible. Deleting a record is not. Irreversible actions default to approve-first. Reversible actions can go up to review-after or full auto depending on the other variables.
   732|
   733|Second variable: velocity. How fast does the action need to happen? A shipment delay notification needs to happen within minutes. A contract review can take hours. A lead response can take tens of minutes. Higher velocity pushes toward full auto or review-after. Lower velocity pushes toward approve-first.
   734|
   735|Third variable: confidence. How sure are we that the agent will make the right call? Confidence comes from testing. If the agent has processed a thousand similar cases with a ninety-five percent accuracy rate, confidence is high. If the agent is new or the use case is novel, confidence is low. Low confidence means approve-first. High confidence means consider full auto or review-after.
   736|
   737|The three variables form a decision matrix. High irreversibility plus low confidence equals approve-first. Low irreversibility plus high velocity plus moderate confidence equals review-after. Low irreversibility plus high confidence equals full auto.
   738|
   739|Here is how this plays out for a function we added recently. The reporting agent sends weekly performance summaries to department heads. The action is sending an email with a PDF attachment. Irreversibility is low. the email can be recalled or followed up with a correction. Velocity is low—weekly reports are not urgent. Confidence is high after three months of testing. So we run it in full auto. The agent generates the report, attaches the PDF, and sends it. No review. No approval. It has been running for six weeks without a mistake.
   740|
   741|Compare that to the customer-facing price quote agent. Same action. sending an email with a document. But irreversibility is high—a wrong price quote is legally binding in many cases. Velocity is moderate—customers expect a quote within hours, not days. Confidence is moderate after testing. So we run it in review-after, but with a twist. The agent sends the quote to the customer and CCs the sales rep. The rep sees the quote immediately and can follow up if anything is wrong. The quote goes out fast, but the rep has eyes on it within seconds.
   742|
   743|The mistake most companies make is choosing one mode for everything. They either lock everything down with approve-first, killing speed, or they let everything run on full auto, creating risk. The right approach is per-function mode selection, reviewed and adjusted monthly.
   744|
   745|I keep a spreadsheet. One row per agent. Columns for function, mode, justification, and incident count. If an agent has zero incidents in its current mode for three months, I consider moving it to a less restrictive mode. If an agent has incidents, I move it to a more restrictive mode.
   746|
   747|The goal is not to eliminate human involvement. The goal is to put human involvement exactly where it adds value and remove it where it adds delay.
   748|
   749|## Chapter 16 — Memory: Why Agents Forget
   750|
   751|I had a conversation with our logistics coordinator agent that made me want to throw my laptop out the window.
   752|
   753|"Check shipment 44982," I said.
   754|
   755|The agent checked. "Shipment 44982 is delayed. The new estimated delivery is Tuesday."
   756|
   757|"What was the original delivery date?"
   758|
   759|The agent paused. Then it called the shipment API again, looking for the original date. It found it. "Monday."
   760|
   761|"Check shipment 44983," I said.
   762|
   763|The agent checked. "Shipment 44983 is on time."
   764|
   765|"And what about the delayed one? 44982?"
   766|
   767|The agent did not know what I was talking about. It had already forgotten about 44982. It asked me to clarify which shipment I meant. I had just told it. Twenty seconds earlier.
   768|
   769|This is the fundamental problem with agent memory. The agents do not remember anything beyond their immediate context window unless you explicitly build memory into the system. The language model has no persistent state. Every interaction starts fresh.
   770|
   771|There are two kinds of memory you need to understand. Short-term memory is the conversation window. The current session. What the agent just did. Long-term memory is persistent storage. Information the agent can access across sessions.
   772|
   773|Short-term memory is handled by the context window. Every time the agent makes a decision, generates a response, or calls a tool, the history of that interaction gets appended to the next request. The model sees everything that happened so far in this session.
   774|
   775|The limit is the context window size. Most models support between 8,000 and 128,000 tokens. A token is roughly three-quarters of a word. So 128,000 tokens is about 96,000 words. That sounds like a lot. It is not.
   776|
   777|Every tool call eats tokens. The tool description. The parameters. The return value. A single CRM lookup can consume 500 tokens. A company enrichment call consumes 1,000. An email draft consumes 1,500. After ten interactions, you have used 30,000 tokens just on tool overhead. The actual conversation is a fraction of that.
   778|
   779|At MIFECO, we handle the short-term memory problem with a sliding window. We keep the last three interactions plus a summary of everything before that. The summary is generated by the agent itself. After every fifth interaction, the agent produces a one-paragraph summary of the conversation so far. That summary replaces the older history in the next context window.
   780|
   781|This approach keeps our costs predictable. Each agent run costs between 2,000 and 5,000 tokens, depending on complexity. Without the sliding window, a long-running agent session could hit 50,000 tokens. At that point, the cost of the conversation exceeds the value of the work being done.
   782|
   783|Long-term memory is a different problem. The agent needs to remember facts across sessions. Customer preferences. Previous orders. Past interactions. This is not something the language model handles naturally. You have to build it.
   784|
   785|I tried several approaches before finding one that works. The first was storing everything in a vector database. Every interaction was embedded and stored. When a new interaction started, the agent searched for relevant past interactions and injected them into the context. This is the standard RAG approach. It worked poorly for us. The agent pulled up irrelevant memories, missed relevant ones, and spent more tokens reading old conversations than handling new ones.
   786|
   787|The second approach was structured memory. Instead of storing raw conversations, we store structured facts. Customer X prefers email over phone. Customer Y has a net-60 payment term. Customer Z always complains about shipping speed. These are key-value pairs stored in a simple database. The agent queries them by customer ID when a session starts.
   788|
   789|This works better. The agent gets exactly the information it needs, no more. The token cost is minimal because the facts are short and targeted. The downside is maintenance. Someone has to write the facts. Our agents can suggest facts to add to memory, but a human reviews and approves them before they go in.
   790|
   791|The third approach, which is what we use now, is a hybrid. Short-term memory uses the sliding window with summaries. Long-term memory uses structured facts with human approval. But we also have a third layer: operational memory.
   792|
   793|Operational memory is the state of the agent's work. What tasks are in progress. What tools have been called. What decisions have been made. This is stored in a JSON object that persists for the duration of a workflow. When the lead responder processes a lead, the operational memory tracks the current step. Step one: CRM check complete. Step two: enrichment in progress. Step three: scoring pending. If the agent gets interrupted, it picks up from the last completed step.
   794|
   795|This matters more than you might think. Agents fail. API calls time out. Model responses are malformed. The user closes the browser. Operational memory means the agent does not start over. It resumes.
   796|
   797|The cost trade-off is straightforward.
   798|
   799|More memory means more tokens per call. Tokens cost money. At our volume, each additional 1,000 tokens of memory costs about three cents. Over twenty thousand runs per month, that is six hundred dollars for a modest increase in memory depth.
   800|
   801|Less memory means the agent forgets things and makes mistakes. Each mistake costs time. Jenny spends twenty minutes fixing an agent error. At her hourly rate, that is about ten dollars per mistake. If the agent makes five mistakes per week due to memory failures, that is two hundred dollars per week.
   802|
   803|The math says invest in memory until the token cost exceeds the mistake cost. For us, that point is around four thousand tokens of context per agent run. That includes the sliding window history, the structured facts, and the operational memory.
   804|
   805|Here is what I recommend for someone starting out. Do not build a vector database on day one. Start with no memory beyond the raw conversation window. See where the agent fails. Add a summary window when conversations exceed ten turns. Add structured facts when the agent starts repeating itself across sessions. Add operational memory when the agent cannot handle interruptions.
   806|
   807|Each layer solves a specific failure mode. Adding all three at once is overengineering. Adding none of them means your agent will forget what it did twenty seconds ago, and you will want to throw your laptop out the window.
   808|
   809|## Chapter 17 — Prompt Design (Not Engineering)
   810|
   811|I hate the term prompt engineering. It implies that writing good prompts is a technical skill on par with writing good code. It is not. Prompting is writing. It is clear communication with an AI system. You do not need to be an engineer to be good at it. You need to be precise.
   812|
   813|The difference between a prompt that works once and a prompt that works reliably is structure. A one-shot prompt is something you write for a specific situation. You are asking the model a question, you get an answer, you move on. A reliable prompt is something you write for production. It runs hundreds or thousands of times. It handles edge cases. It produces consistent output.
   814|
   815|At MIFECO, every production prompt follows the same template. Role, rules, examples. Three sections. No deviations.
   816|
   817|The role section defines who the agent is and what it is supposed to do. I wrote earlier about the lead responder's role. Let me show you the exact text.
   818|
   819|"You are a lead qualification and outreach assistant for MIFECO, a logistics technology company. You work for the sales team. Your job is to process incoming leads from the website contact form. You research the lead and their company, score the lead on a scale of 1 to 5, and draft a personalized initial email. You do not send the email. You submit it for human review. You never make up information about a lead or company. If you cannot find reliable information, you note the gap and proceed with what you have."
   820|
   821|That is the role section. It establishes identity, function, boundaries, and failure mode. It tells the agent what to do, what not to do, and what to do when things go wrong.
   822|
   823|The role section is not a personality. It is a job description. I do not tell the agent to be friendly, helpful, or professional. Those are vague, and the agent interprets them differently every time. I tell the agent exactly what steps to follow and exactly what constraints to respect.
   824|
   825|The rules section lists constraints. Every rule is a specific behavior, not a general principle.
   826|
   827|Rule one: always check CRM for existing records before doing any research. Rule two: if the CRM check returns a record with contact date within thirty days, mark as duplicate and skip. Rule three: use the company enrichment tool before scoring. Rule four: the score field must be an integer between 1 and 5. Rule five: the email draft must include the lead's specific question or comment in the first paragraph. Rule six: if any tool returns an error, note the error in the output and continue with available data.
   828|
   829|Each rule exists because an earlier version of the agent violated it. Rule one exists because the agent once enriched a company that was already in CRM, wasting a tool call and returning redundant data. Rule three exists because the agent once scored a lead before looking up the company, giving a high score to someone with no discernible company. Rule six exists because the agent once failed silently when the enrichment tool timed out, producing an empty profile without flagging the issue.
   830|
   831|The rules are a record of failures. Every time the agent makes a mistake, I add a rule to prevent it from happening again. The rules section grows over time. It started with two rules. It now has fourteen across all agents. Not every rule applies to every agent.
   832|
   833|The examples section is the most powerful part of the prompt. I include three to five complete examples of the agent doing its job. Each example shows the input, the thought process, the tool calls, and the final output. The examples are real. They come from actual agent runs that were approved by a human.
   834|
   835|Here is a condensed example from the lead responder prompt.
   836|
   837|Input: John Smith, Acme Logistics, john@acme.com, "We need help with international shipping tracking."
   838|
   839|Thought: This is a logistics company. They have a specific need. Medium score potential. Check CRM first.
   840|
   841|Tool call: CRM search for Acme Logistics. Result: no existing record.
   842|
   843|Tool call: Company enrichment for Acme Logistics. Result: 200 employees, logistics sector, founded 2018, estimated revenue 50M.
   844|
   845|Lead score: 4 out of 5. Medium-high priority. Established company, clear need, relevant industry.
   846|
   847|Draft: "Hi John, thanks for reaching out. You mentioned international shipping tracking. MIFECO's logistics platform supports real-time tracking across 40 carriers globally. Would you be available for a brief call this week to discuss your requirements?"
   848|
   849|Output: Score 4, draft attached, no duplicates found.
   850|
   851|That example took me five minutes to write. It has saved me hours of debugging. The agent now produces outputs that look exactly like that example ninety-three percent of the time.
   852|
   853|The template works because it replaces ambiguity with structure. Without the role section, the agent does not know its boundaries. Without the rules section, the agent makes the same mistakes repeatedly. Without the examples, the agent invents its own output format and it changes every time.
   854|
   855|The difference between a works-once prompt and a works-reliably prompt is the investment in rules and examples. A works-once prompt has a role and a single instruction. It works for the first call and degrades from there. A works-reliably prompt has explicit rules for every known failure mode and concrete examples that anchor the output format.
   856|
   857|I spend about an hour per week on prompt maintenance. I review the logs from the previous week, identify patterns in agent failures, and update the rules or examples for the affected prompts. This is not prompt engineering. It is editing. I am making the instructions clearer based on where the agent went wrong.
   858|
   859|The single biggest improvement I made to our prompts was removing ambiguity. I replaced "be thorough" with "call the enrichment tool and the scoring tool for every lead." I replaced "be careful with pricing" with "never include pricing in the first email." I replaced "prioritize high-value leads" with "score each lead 1-5 based on company size and message intent."
   860|
   861|Clear instructions produce reliable agents. Vague instructions produce unreliable agents that occasionally get lucky. The second generation of our prompts was half the length of the first and twice as effective. Brevity forces precision.
   862|
   863|## Chapter 18 — Testing Without Breaking
   864|
   865|I deployed an agent to production that immediately sent a hundred emails to the wrong people. Not test emails. Real emails. To real customers. With wrong information.
   866|
   867|It was a reporting agent. It was supposed to send weekly summaries to department heads. I had tested it in a sandbox. It worked perfectly. I promoted it to production. The first batch went to the wrong email list. The agent read the distribution list from our CRM, but it read the internal field name instead of the email field. Every department head got someone else's report.
   868|
   869|The mistake was mine. I did not test with production data. I tested with mock data where the email field and the name field happened to have the same values. The agent looked correct in the sandbox and wrong in reality.
   870|
   871|That incident cost me a day of apologizing and a system I call three-stage testing. I have used it for every agent since. No failures in production for over six months.
   872|
   873|Stage one is safe testing. The agent runs in a fully isolated environment. It has no access to real tools, real data, or real APIs. Every tool call returns mock data. You can test as aggressively as you want without consequences.
   874|
   875|Our safe environment is a separate database with synthetic records. Fake customers, fake emails, fake orders. The agent processes these and produces outputs. I check whether the outputs are structurally correct. Does the lead responder produce the right JSON format? Does the logistics coordinator call the right tools in the right order? Does the contract reviewer flag the right clauses?
   876|
   877|Safe testing catches format errors, tool call errors, and prompt parsing errors. It does not catch logic errors because the mock data is too clean. Real data is messy. Mock data is tidy. A prompt that works perfectly on tidy mock data can collapse on the first real input with a missing field.
   878|
   879|Stage two is correct testing. The agent runs in a staging environment that mirrors production. It has access to real tools but operates on a copy of the data. The staging database is a snapshot from the previous week. The email API is set to a test mode that captures all outbound messages without delivering them. The CRM is a sandbox instance with copied records.
   880|
   881|Correct testing answers two questions. Does the agent make the right decision given real data? Does the agent produce the right output for a human to review?
   882|
   883|I run stage two for at least fifty agent runs before moving to stage three. Fifty runs is enough to hit the common edge cases. Missing fields. Duplicate records. Unusual formatting. Special characters. Every time the agent fails in stage two, I fix the prompt or add a rule before restarting the count.
   884|
   885|One example. During correct testing of the lead responder, the agent received a lead with a company name that included a trademark symbol. The enrichment tool could not find the company because the symbol was in the query. The agent returned a partial profile and scored the lead based on incomplete data. We added a rule to strip special characters from company names before calling the enrichment tool. Problem solved in stage two, never seen in production.
   886|
   887|Stage three is useful testing. The agent runs in production but with a human watchdog. Every output is reviewed before any action is taken. No automated sends. No automated updates. The agent works, but a human gates every output.
   888|
   889|Stage three lasts one week. Seven days of production data, real conditions, human oversight. I look for two things. First, does the agent produce useful output that passes human review at least ninety percent of the time? Second, does the agent handle the unexpected inputs that did not appear in stage two?
   890|
   891|The first week of useful testing for the lead responder revealed a problem we had missed. The agent handled English leads well. Spanish leads produced lower quality outputs. The score was often wrong because the agent could not assess the intent from the translated message. We added a language detection step. If the lead message is not in English, the agent flags it for manual handling and skips scoring. That rule went in during the useful testing week.
   892|
   893|The staging pattern is the infrastructure that enables this testing. We have three environments. Dev is for safe testing. Staging is for correct testing. Prod is for useful testing. Each environment is identical in code and different in data access and tool permissions.
   894|
   895|Dev uses mock APIs. All tool calls return fake data. The agent can call any tool without consequences.
   896|
   897|Staging uses real APIs with sandbox credentials. The CRM sandbox. The email test mode. The calendar test tenant. The data is real but the effects are contained.
   898|
   899|Prod uses real APIs with production credentials but with human approval gates. The agent can suggest anything, but nothing executes without a human saying yes.

{"content": "   901|Promoting an agent from one stage to the next requires passing a checklist. The checklist is specific and short.
   902|
   903|For stage one to stage two: the agent completes twenty safe test runs with no structural errors. All tool calls are valid. All outputs match the expected format. No crashes.
   904|
   905|For stage two to stage three: the agent completes fifty staging runs with at least ninety percent correct decisions. Correct means a human reviewer would approve the output without modification. The remaining ten percent are logged and categorized.
   906|
   907|For stage three to production: the agent completes one week of useful testing with at least ninety percent human approval rate. No incidents involving data loss, wrong recipient, or incorrect pricing output.
   908|
   909|The checklist lives in a shared document. Every agent has a row. Every promotion has a date and a reviewer name. Nothing moves without a sign-off.
   910|
   911|The pre-live checklist is the last gate before an agent becomes fully autonomous. It has five items.
   912|
   913|One: all rules from the testing phase are documented in the prompt. Two: all tools have correct permission tiers. Three: a human reviewer is assigned for the first month. Four: rollback plan exists. If the agent fails, we can disable it and restore the previous workflow within fifteen minutes. Five: monitoring is configured. Metrics are being collected. Alerts are set.
   914|
   915|I do not skip items on this checklist. I have a scar from the time I skipped item four. The reporting agent went to production, sent wrong emails, I had no rollback plan, and it took four hours to undo the damage. The rollback plan is now item four and it is non-negotiable.
   916|
   917|## Chapter 19 — Monitoring: How to Know It's Working
   918|
   919|I had an agent running for three weeks before I realized it was failing half the time. The agent was supposed to check shipment statuses and flag delays. It was running, it was logging, it was generating outputs. No one complained. No alerts fired. But when I finally looked at the data, forty-seven percent of the tool calls were failing silently.
   920|
   921|The shipping API had changed its response format. The agent expected a field called "estimated_delivery." The API now returned "eta." Every call succeeded at the HTTP level and returned a 200 status code. But the agent's enrichment step received null for the delivery date because the field name did not match. The agent logged "No data found" and moved on. No error. No alert. No human noticed for three weeks.
   922|
   923|That is the monitoring problem. Agents look like they are working when they are not. They do not crash. They produce output. The output is just wrong. You need visibility into what the agent is actually doing, not just that it is running.
   924|
   925|I now track four categories of metrics for every agent. Volume, accuracy, cost, and latency. Each category answers a specific question about agent health.
   926|
   927|Volume metrics answer the question: is the agent doing the work? I track runs per hour, runs per agent, and runs by outcome category. Outcome categories are completed, failed, escalated, and rejected. Completed means the agent finished its workflow. Failed means the agent hit an error it could not recover from. Escalated means the agent handed off to a human. Rejected means a human rejected the agent's output.
   928|
   929|The volume dashboard shows a bar chart for the last seven days. Each day has four colored bars for the four outcomes. If the failed bar starts growing, something is broken. If the rejected bar grows, the prompt needs updating. If the completed bar stays flat while lead volume increases, the agent is bottlenecked.
   930|
   931|Accuracy metrics answer the question: is the agent doing the work correctly? I track human approval rate, correction rate, and error rate. Approval rate is the percentage of agent outputs that pass human review without changes. Correction rate is the percentage that need edits before approval. Error rate is the percentage that are rejected entirely.
   932|
   933|The lead responder's approval rate is ninety-three percent. The correction rate is five percent. The error rate is two percent. Those numbers have been stable for four months. If approval rate drops below eighty-five percent, I pause the agent and investigate.
   934|
   935|Accuracy metrics are the most important because they are the only direct measure of agent quality. Volume metrics tell you the agent is busy. Accuracy metrics tell you the agent is useful.
   936|
   937|Cost metrics answer the question: is the agent worth running? I track cost per run, cost by tool, and cost by model. Cost per run is the total token cost divided by the number of completed runs. Cost by tool shows which tool calls are eating the most tokens. Cost by model shows which models are cheapest for which tasks.
   938|
   939|The average cost per lead responder run is two point three cents. The average cost per logistics coordinator run is four point one cents. The average cost per contract reviewer run is eight point two cents. If the cost per run spikes, something changed. Maybe the model increased prices. Maybe the agent is making more tool calls than expected. Maybe the context window is growing.
   940|
   941|I set cost alerts at two times the average. If any agent exceeds twice its normal cost per run for a full day, I get a notification.
   942|
   943|Latency metrics answer the question: is the agent fast enough? I track end-to-end run time, per-tool latency, and queue wait time. End-to-end is how long a complete agent run takes from input to output. Per-tool latency is how long each tool call takes. Queue wait time is how long outputs sit before human review.
   944|
   945|The lead responder completes in an average of eight seconds. The logistics coordinator averages fourteen seconds. The contract reviewer averages forty-five seconds because it uses a slower, more capable model. If the lead responder takes more than fifteen seconds, something is wrong. Probably a slow API call or a context window that grew too large.
   946|
   947|My dashboard is a single Grafana page. Four rows of panels, one row per metric category. Each row has a sparkline for the last thirty days and a current value. Red, yellow, green thresholds are set for each metric. Green is normal. Yellow means investigate. Red means act.
   948|
   949|The dashboard auto-refreshes every sixty seconds. I check it twice a day. Morning coffee and end of day. Each check takes about thirty seconds. I scan for red panels first, then yellow, then glance at the trends.
   950|
   951|The most important panel is the one that shows the last twenty-four hours of failed runs with their error messages. This panel is my early warning system. If I see a new error message, I investigate immediately. Most errors are transient. API timeouts, rate limits, network blips. But a new error message is often the first sign of a real problem.
   952|
   953|I learned to watch for patterns, not individual failures. One failed run is noise. Five failed runs with the same error in an hour is a signal. My dashboard flags patterns automatically. If the same error appears more than three times in an hour, the panel turns yellow.
   954|
   955|The logging infrastructure behind the dashboard is straightforward. Every agent run produces a structured log entry. Tool calls, decisions, outcomes, timestamps, costs. The logs go to a central database. The database powers the dashboard queries. The whole stack costs about fifty dollars per month in hosting.
   956|
   957|The alternative is no monitoring, which is what I had for the first three months. I thought the agent was working. It was not. I thought I would notice if something went wrong. I did not. The forty-seven percent failure rate sat there for three weeks because there was no dashboard, no alerts, and no one looking at the data.
   958|
   959|You do not need a fancy observability platform. You need three things. A log of every agent run with structured fields. A dashboard that shows volume, accuracy, cost, and latency. An alert that fires when any metric goes outside its normal range. That is it. Build that before you deploy your second agent. The first agent you can watch manually. The second agent will run unsupervised and you will not know if it is failing until someone complains.
   960|
   961|## Chapter 20 — Case Study: Weekend to Production
   962|
   963|I want to give you a complete case study of one agent from concept to production. Not a sanitized version. The exact timeline, the decisions, what went right, what went wrong, and what it cost. This is the most honest accounting I can provide.
   964|
   965|The agent is our escalation handler. It takes support tickets that have been flagged as unresolved by the first-line support team and routes them to the right person with a summary and suggested resolution. Before the agent, this was done by a senior support person named Carlos. He spent about three hours per day reading escalated tickets, figuring out who should handle them, and writing summaries for the assignee.
   966|
   967|I decided to automate this on a Friday afternoon. Bad idea, but it made for a good experiment.
   968|
   969|Friday 4 PM: I wrote the first version of the system prompt. I used the template from chapter seventeen. Role: escalation routing assistant. Rules: always read the full ticket history, identify the most relevant team, write a one-paragraph summary, suggest a resolution category. Examples: three real escalated tickets that Carlos had handled.
   970|
   971|Friday 6 PM: I built the first tool. Just one. A team lookup tool that returns the right team based on the ticket category. Billing issues go to finance. Technical issues go to engineering. Account issues go to account management. The tool had three parameters: ticket ID, category, and urgency.
   972|
   973|Friday 8 PM: I ran the first safe test. Ten mock tickets. The agent picked the right team for eight of them. The two failures were both tickets about account access, which could be either engineering or account management. The agent picked account management both times. Carlos would have picked engineering because account access is a technical issue, not a policy issue. I added a rule: "If the ticket involves login, authentication, or access, route to engineering."
   974|
   975|Friday 10 PM: I ran the second safe test with the updated prompt. Ten more mock tickets. Nine correct. The failure was a ticket about a billing dispute that was actually caused by a software bug. The agent sent it to finance. I decided this was too subtle for a rule. I added it to the examples instead, showing a similar case where the agent should call both the finance and engineering teams.
   976|
   977|Saturday 9 AM: I set up the staging environment. I cloned last week's ticket data from production into a staging database. I configured the email tool to capture outputs instead of sending them. I set the CRM integration to sandbox mode. Total setup time: forty-five minutes.
   978|
   979|Saturday 10 AM: Stage two testing began. I ran the agent against fifty real escalated tickets from the previous week. I knew what Carlos had done for each one, so I could compare.
   980|
   981|The results were sobering. The agent matched Carlos's routing decision thirty-eight out of fifty times. That is seventy-six percent. Not bad for a first attempt, but not good enough for production. I analyzed the twelve mismatches.
   982|
   983|Five were cases where the ticket had multiple categories and the agent picked one while Carlos had split the ticket and routed to two teams. I added a tool that could route to multiple teams.
   984|
   985|Four were cases where the ticket language was ambiguous. The agent did not ask clarifying questions because I had not told it to. I added a rule: "If the ticket category is unclear, flag it for human review rather than guessing."
   986|
   987|Three were cases where the agent had misinterpreted the priority. A ticket marked "urgent" by the customer was actually a low-priority request. Carlos knew this customer was dramatic. The agent did not. I added a rule to deprioritize tickets from customers with a history of marking everything urgent, based on a pattern in the CRM history.
   988|
   989|Saturday 4 PM: I ran stage two again with the updated prompt and the multi-team tool. Forty-eight out of fifty matched Carlos's decisions. Ninety-six percent. The two failures were edge cases. One was a ticket in French. The other was a ticket about a product that had been discontinued, which required a specific handling process. I added both to the examples.
   990|
   991|Saturday 6 PM: I decided to move to stage three. Useful testing in production with human review.
   992|
   993|Here is what went right. The staging environment caught the major issues before they hit production. The multi-team routing problem would have caused a lot of confusion if it had gone live without being caught. The ambiguous language rule prevented the agent from guessing on unclear tickets.
   994|
   995|Here is what went wrong. I skipped the pre-live checklist. Specifically, I did not set up the monitoring dashboard. I told myself I would do it Monday. Sunday afternoon, the agent processed a ticket that had a corrupted attachment. The agent read the attachment, got a parsing error, and logged a generic failure message. But it did not flag the failure anywhere I could see. Carlos manually routed that ticket three hours later, wondering why the agent had skipped it. I found out Monday morning.
   996|
   997|The monitoring gap meant I lost a day of data. I could not see how the agent performed on Sunday. I had to reconstruct from the logs manually. I set up the dashboard Monday morning and it has been running ever since.
   998|
   999|Sunday 10 AM: I reviewed the first batch of agent outputs. Fifty-two tickets processed overnight. Human approval rate was ninety-four percent. Three outputs needed edits. All three were cases where the agent could not determine the right team and flagged for review, which was the correct behavior. The edits were minor. The agent had routed correctly but the summary was missing a key detail in each case.
  1000|
  1001|Sunday 2 PM: I expanded the agent's tools. I added a ticket history reader that pulls the last five interactions on a ticket. The agent was writing summaries without enough context about what had already been tried. With the history reader, the summaries improved noticeably.
  1002|
  1003|Sunday 6 PM: Carlos reviewed the day's work. He approved forty-nine out of fifty-two. He noted that the agent was better than he expected at categorizing technical issues and worse at handling billing edge cases. I added two more billing examples to the prompt.
  1004|
  1005|Monday 9 AM: The agent went to production with full human-in-the-loop mode. Carlos reviewed every output before routing. His workload went from three hours per day to one hour. The other two hours went to higher-value support work.
  1006|
  1007|The cost breakdown for the weekend.
  1008|
  1009|My time: fourteen hours across Saturday and Sunday. Prompt writing, tool building, testing, debugging. At my internal rate, about two thousand eight hundred dollars in labor cost.
  1010|
  1011|Infrastructure: zero additional cost. The agent ran on our existing staging and production environments. No new servers, no new tools, no new licenses.
  1012|
  1013|API costs for testing: about twelve dollars in token costs across all test runs. Fifty tickets at an average of four cents per run in staging. Another fifty-two tickets at six cents per run in production with human review.
  1014|
  1015|Total cost: about two thousand eight hundred twelve dollars and fourteen hours of my weekend.
  1016|
  1017|The ongoing cost: about three hundred dollars per month in API tokens. Carlos now spends one hour per day on escalation instead of three. At his salary, that saves about eighteen thousand dollars per year. The agent pays for itself in about two months.
  1018|
  1019|What I would do differently. I would set up the monitoring dashboard before the first production run. I would run the first batch of staging tests on Thursday instead of Saturday, so I could take a break in between. I would not add the multi-team tool in the middle of stage two testing. Adding a tool mid-test invalidates the results. I should have restarted the fifty-run count after adding the tool.
  1020|
  1021|What I would do the same. Start with one tool and add more as needed. Use the exact prompt template. Compare every output against a human baseline. Keep the first deployment in review mode. Do not skip the pre-live checklist. wait, I did skip it, and that is the one thing I would fix.
  1022|
  1023|The escalation handler has been running for six months now. It routes about eight hundred tickets per month. Carlos approves ninety-two percent of them. The remaining eight percent are edge cases that get routed manually. The agent frees up about forty hours of Carlos's time per month. He spends that time on process improvements and training instead of ticket sorting.
  1024|
  1025|but it was real, and it worked. That weekend taught me that the hardest part of building an agent isn't the technology. It's deciding to start.

  1029|# PART III — From One Agent to an Autonomous Operation
  1030|
  1031|
  1032|## Chapter 21 — Multi-Agent Architecture
  1033|
  1034|The lead came in at 3:14 PM. My first agent caught it, researched the company, drafted a personalized email, and sent it. All in under four minutes. I sat back and thought: I've done it. One agent to rule them all.
  1035|
  1036|Two weeks later, that same agent sent a follow-up to a prospect who had already replied saying they weren't interested. It cost me the deal. The prospect wrote back: "I literally told you no. Are you even listening?"
  1037|
  1038|That was the moment I learned why one agent can't do everything.
  1039|
  1040|The problem is obvious once you think about it. A single agent has one brain, one context window, one set of instructions. When you ask it to capture leads, qualify them, write emails, update a CRM, check for duplicates, monitor replies, and report on results . you're asking it to be good at everything. No single person can do all those jobs well. Why would an agent be different?
  1041|
  1042|The lead capture part needs speed and breadth. Grab any form submission, any email, any LinkedIn message, and stuff it into the pipeline. Don't overthink it. The qualification part needs judgment. Is this company a real fit? Do they have budget? Are they just kicking tires? The outreach part needs tone and timing. The CRM part needs precision. The monitoring part needs patience.
  1043|
  1044|These are different skills. Different priorities. Different failure modes.
  1045|
  1046|I found this out the hard way. My monolithic agent handled everything for about three weeks. Then the cracks showed. It sent a follow-up too early. It logged a duplicate contact because the name was spelled differently. It spent too long researching a lead that was clearly spam. It got confused about which email thread was which.
  1047|
  1048|The fix is specialization. You don't hire one person to run your entire business. You hire a salesperson, a marketer, an operations person, a customer support person. Each has a focused role. Each knows what they're responsible for. Each has tools specific to their job.
  1049|
  1050|Agents work the same way.
  1051|
  1052|I rebuilt the system with three specialized agents. A capture agent that just watches for new leads and creates records. A qualification agent that reviews each lead against my criteria and decides whether to pursue it. An outreach agent that handles the communication. Three agents, three jobs, three sets of instructions.
  1053|
  1054|The capture agent is simple. It watches the contact form, checks for new emails from unknown senders, and monitors a few lead sources. When it finds something, it creates a record in the pipeline and passes it to the qualification agent. That's it. It doesn't write emails. It doesn't check for quality. It just captures.
  1055|
  1056|The qualification agent takes the raw lead and evaluates it. It checks the company size, the industry, the job title of the contact, the language in their message. It scores the lead and decides: hot, warm, cold, or spam. Hot leads go straight to outreach. Warm leads go to a nurture sequence. Cold leads get filed. Spam gets deleted. This agent has authority to make these decisions without me.
  1057|
  1058|The outreach agent only talks to leads that have been qualified. It writes the first email, schedules follow-ups, monitors replies, and updates the pipeline status. It doesn't decide who to contact. It doesn't judge quality. It just communicates.
  1059|
  1060|This is the supervisor pattern. One agent doesn't tell the others what to do . the architecture does. The pipeline itself enforces the flow. Data moves from one agent to the next through a queue. Each agent has a defined input and output. If an agent fails, the queue holds the work until it recovers.
  1061|
  1062|The difference was immediate. The capture agent never misses a lead because it has one job and one job only. The qualification agent makes better decisions because it sees the full context without being distracted by outreach tasks. The outreach agent communicates more naturally because it isn't juggling capture and qualification at the same time.
  1063|
  1064|Duplicates almost disappeared. Not because I wrote dedup logic . because the qualification agent had enough context to recognize when a lead was already in the pipeline. Before, the monolithic agent would create a new record every time it saw the same company from a different source. Now the qualification agent checks existing records before scoring.
  1065|
  1066|The architecture also made debugging easier. When something went wrong, I knew which agent to check. An email formatting issue? That's the outreach agent. A lead that shouldn't have been qualified? That's the qualifier. A missing record? That's the capture agent. Instead of digging through one giant log file, I could look at the specific agent's logs.
  1067|
  1068|Here's the part that surprised me: specialization also made the agents cheaper. Each agent uses a different model. The capture agent runs on a cheap, fast model because it just needs to extract text and write records. The qualification agent runs on a mid-tier model because it needs judgment. The outreach agent runs on the best model I can afford because tone and timing matter. I'm not paying for a top-tier model to do data entry.
  1069|
  1070|The downside is complexity. You go from one agent to three. You need a way for them to communicate. You need to define those interfaces. You need error handling between stages. You need monitoring across multiple agents. It's more work to set up. But it's more reliable in production.
  1071|
  1072|If you're starting out, build one agent first. Get it working. Then break it into pieces as the cracks appear. Don't design a multi-agent system on day one. Design one agent, then watch where it struggles, and split those responsibilities off. The cracks tell you where the seams should be.
  1073|
  1074|My first agent cracked at week three. That was enough to teach me that one brain can't do everything. A team of specialists beats a generalist every time.
  1075|
  1076|The question isn't whether you need multiple agents. It's when you'll realize you do.
  1077|
  1078|
  1079|## Chapter 22 — The Orchestrator Pattern
  1080|
  1081|The three-agent system worked better than the monolith. But I still had a problem. Who routes the work? When the capture agent finds a lead, how does it know the qualification agent is ready? What happens when the qualification agent is busy with another lead? What if the outreach agent crashes while sending an email?
  1082|
  1083|I needed a traffic cop. Someone who delegates, monitors, and handles exceptions. That's the orchestrator.
  1084|
  1085|The orchestrator pattern is simple on paper. One supervisor agent that doesn't do actual work. Instead, it receives requests, decides which worker agent should handle them, passes the work along, and waits for the result. If the worker fails, the orchestrator retries or escalates. If the worker succeeds, the orchestrator decides what happens next.
  1086|
  1087|Think of it like a project manager who doesn't code, doesn't design, doesn't write copy. The PM just makes sure the right person gets the right task at the right time. That's the orchestrator.
  1088|
  1089|I built mine using a pattern I call the router loop. The orchestrator runs in a continuous loop. Each cycle, it checks the incoming queue for new work. If there's work, it reads the task, checks its type, and routes it to the appropriate worker. Then it stores the result and checks for the next task. The loop repeats every few seconds.
  1090|
  1091|The workers don't talk to each other. They don't know the other agents exist. The capture agent outputs a lead record and forgets about it. The qualification agent picks it up from the queue, processes it, and outputs a scored lead. The outreach agent picks the scored lead and handles the communication. The orchestrator manages the handoffs.
  1092|
  1093|This is how Hermes Agent works under the hood. Hermes has a supervisor that receives a user's request . "check my email, find anything urgent, draft replies" — and breaks it into subtasks. Check email is one subtask. Evaluate urgency is another. Draft replies is a third. The supervisor dispatches each subtask to a specialized worker, collects the results, and assembles the final response.
  1094|
  1095|The key insight is that the orchestrator doesn't need to be smart. It needs to be reliable. The smart work happens in the workers. The orchestrator just needs to route correctly, handle timeouts, and manage retries. A simple loop with a switch statement handles most of it.
  1096|
  1097|Here's what my orchestrator looks like in practice:
  1098|
  1099|The capture agent finds a new lead and pushes it to the new-leads queue. The orchestrator polls this queue every five seconds. When it finds a new entry, it creates a task record with a unique ID, the lead data, and a status of "pending." It assigns the task to the qualification agent and updates the status to "processing."
